papers_read.title_as_printed: A deep learning model for the detection of various dementia and MCI pathologies based on resting-state electroencephalography data: A retrospective multicentre study (Watanabe et al., Neural Networks 171 (2024) 242-250)
Mild Cognitive Impairment detection based on EEG and HRV data (Boudaya et al., Digital Signal Processing 147 (2024) 104399)

what_each_reports.P-62: MNet deep CNN on 19-channel resting eyes-closed clinical EEG, trained at Osaka University Hospital only. Healthy volunteers vs DEMENTIA (AD+DLB+iNPH): bACC 0.927 +/- 0.015 internal (5-fold CV), external bACC 0.805 at Hospital K and 0.920 at Hospital N (ensemble). No healthy-vs-MCI classification is reported: the only MCI result is pathology subtyping WITHIN MCI (AD vs DLB vs iNPH), bACC 0.715, ROC AUC 0.847, Hospital O.
what_each_reports.P-83: Hybrid voting ML (SVM+GB+RF) on EEG (Emotiv 14-channel) plus HRV (Polar H10) features recorded during CERAD sub-tests, 15 participants (8 MCI/7 HC per the abstract), segment-level 75/25 shuffled split. MCI vs HC average accuracy across CERAD tests 93.86% (sens 93.87%, spec 93.53%); best test T1 97.43% (AUC 94.91%); LOOCV T1 96.14%.

quantity_a: Balanced accuracy of a resting-state EEG CNN for healthy volunteers vs overt dementia (AD, DLB, iNPH) in external Japanese hospital cohorts; MCI appears only as a within-MCI pathology subtyping task
quantity_b: Segment-level accuracy of an EEG+HRV feature ensemble for MCI (amnestic and non-amnestic) vs healthy controls during CERAD cognitive tasks, 15 German participants, internal shuffled split
incompatible_if_same: Not assessable as a conflict: the 0.805-0.920 range belongs to the dementia-vs-healthy comparison, which P-83 never studies, and P-83's MCI-vs-HC comparison is never studied by P-62. Even as raw numbers, 0.920 bACC and 93.86% accuracy are close, and neither paper claims a value the other refutes.

gates.task: mismatch: P-62's 0.805-0.920 is healthy vs dementia (not T1 MCI detection); P-83 is MCI vs HC (T1)
gates.dataset_family: mismatch: P-62 Osaka/Kochi/Nippon Life hospital EEG archives; P-83 own Magdeburg cohort of 15. The record itself has dataset_equal='No'
gates.validation_tier: mismatch: the claimed P-62 values are external-hospital tests (V4); P-83 uses a shuffled 75/25 split of EEG segments from 15 people (internal, with subject overlap between train and test not excluded)
gates.modality_family: partial: both EEG, but P-83 fuses EEG with HRV and records during cognitive tasks, P-62 resting clinical EEG

endpoint_and_metric: incompatible: different comparison (dementia vs healthy against MCI vs healthy) and different metric (balanced accuracy vs accuracy at segment level)
performance_validity: flag applies to P-83 in part: its best result is 97.43% accuracy on internal validation with n=15 and no external cohort, and the 93.86% quoted in the record is the average of the same internal segment-level evaluation. The registry did not trip the automatic test because it recorded the average. Any performance comparison resting on P-83 is excluded under Section 2.
independence: Independent: different groups (Osaka University; Sfax/Magdeburg/Toulouse), different cohorts.
grounds: P-62's 0.805 and 0.920 are balanced accuracies for healthy volunteers vs dementia patients at the external hospitals, not for MCI detection, so the record's 'on T1' label is wrong.
P-62 reports no healthy-vs-MCI result; its MCI figure (bACC 0.715) is AD vs DLB vs iNPH subtyping within MCI.
P-83 reports MCI vs HC accuracy in 15 participants, so the two papers report on different comparisons, populations and metrics.
The dataset-family and validation-tier gates also fail with no waiver on record, and P-83's own best result (97.43%, n=15, internal) meets the performance-validity exclusion.

evidence_quotes.quote: the DCNN achieved a balanced accuracy (bACC) of 0.927 in classifying individuals as healthy (n = 69) or as having AD, DLB, or iNPH (n = 188). The model demonstrated robustness across institutions, maintaining bACCs of 0.805 for data from Hospital #2 (n = 73) and 0.920 at Hospital #3 (n = 139).
Notably, it also identified MCI pathologies with a bACC of 0.715 for Hospital #1 (n = 83), despite being trained on overt dementia cases instead of MCI cases.
Importantly, data obtained from individuals with MCI and data collected at Hospital K and Hospital N were not used for training and were included only in the test sets.
Our dataset includes 15 subjects who were randomly assigned to training and testing groups of 7 HC and 8 MCI, respectively.
An average accuracy of 93.86%, a sensitivity of 93.87%, and a specificity of 93.53% are achieved.

For each test, we separated our data into 75% for the training set and 25% for the testing set. To boost the effectiveness of ML model accuracy and to reduce the rate of overfitting, we applied the shuffling strategy throughout the data partitioning process.
the first test called "Verbal fluency" related to the executive function had the highest accuracy (97.43%).

record_defects: claim_a 'P-62: bACC 0.805-0.920 on T1' mislabels the task: these are healthy vs dementia (AD+DLB+iNPH) external-hospital balanced accuracies, not MCI detection.
validation_comparable='Yes' is wrong: P-62's quoted values are external-site tests; P-83 is a shuffled internal split of segments from 15 people.
The earlier note 'Confirmed genuine: Same metric type (Acc)' is wrong: P-62 reports balanced accuracy, P-83 accuracy.
The bridging-evidence list consists of papers from other modalities and tasks (e.g. MRS, MR elastography, nomograms) described as 'comparable task/dataset family'; none bears on this pair.
The registry's Best_Metric for P-83 (Acc 93.86) is the cross-test average; the paper's reported best is 97.43%, which would trip the performance-validity test.
what_would_change_the_verdict: Only a P-62 healthy-vs-MCI classification result (not present in the article; supplementary tables were not in the extract) set against P-83 on a comparable validation tier, and P-83 would still fall under the performance-validity exclusion.
